description_en: Dried bark of an evergreen Asian tree, used in Unani medicine as an astringent for bleeding and discharges.
safety_note: The monograph itself notes possible abdominal heaviness, nausea and constipation on an empty stomach. No independent safety data found in the sources fetched.
evidence_note: Only taxonomy was confirmed from a stub page; no human clinical evidence was located.

description_en: Dried fruit of a thorny shrub used traditionally in South Asia as an emetic-type and respiratory remedy.
safety_note: The monograph warns that excess may cause vomiting, indigestion and loss of appetite. The plant is described as having fish-poisoning and snail-killing properties; no detailed human toxicology was found.
evidence_note: Lab studies report antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, antidiabetic and lipid-lowering activity; no human trials were found.

uses_modern.meaning: roughness or hoarseness of the throat

description_en: Unripe green banana, a common food starch also used traditionally for diarrhoea and stomach complaints.
evidence_note: Wikipedia confirms its role as a staple cooked food; no clinical evidence for the listed Unani uses was found in fetched sources.

botanical_name: Quercus infectoria (galls induced by gall wasps)
common_name_en: Oak gall (Aleppo oak / Dyer's oak gall)
description_en: Tannin-rich growths on oak twigs, used as a strong astringent for diarrhoea, bleeding and discharges.
safety_note: Reviews advise against long-term high-dose intake; the high tannin content can irritate the stomach and cause nausea and vomiting.
evidence_note: Reviews report mostly animal and lab findings (antibacterial, antioxidant, anti-inflammatory); human clinical evidence is very thin, with at most one clinical trial.

description_en: Dried ripe fruit of an evergreen tree prized for fragrant flowers, used traditionally for sexual and bowel complaints.
evidence_note: Wikipedia cites a 2012 review but reports no clinical findings; the fruit pulp is edible.

category_unani: Muhallil-e-Waram (anti-inflammatory); Muqawwi-e-Asab (nerve tonic); Mufatteh Sudad (deobstruent); Kasir-e-Riyah (carminative)
description_en: Aromatic gum-resin from a thorny desert tree, long used in Ayurvedic and Unani medicine for joints and lipids.
safety_note: Memorial Sloan Kettering lists headache, nausea, belching, loose stools and rash; guggul may induce CYP3A4 (reducing some drugs' effect), may alter thyroid tests, and has been linked to liver enzyme rises. Pregnancy safety not established.
evidence_note: Human evidence for cholesterol lowering is mixed, with several trials showing no benefit or raised LDL; evidence for arthritis and haemorrhoids is lacking. The species is critically endangered.

common_name_en: Neem gum (margosa / Indian lilac tree gum)
description_en: Natural gum that oozes from neem tree bark, used in pharmaceuticals as a binder and traditionally for skin ailments.
safety_note: Neem oil can be toxic or fatal to small children; MSK describes serious poisoning from swallowed oil. Neem is reported to risk miscarriage and infertility and may lower blood sugar. These findings concern neem products generally, not specifically the gum.
evidence_note: Wikipedia states there is insufficient clinical evidence for neem's medicinal benefits; the gum is mainly documented as a pharmaceutical excipient.

uses_modern.meaning: hysterical suffocation of the womb (uterine hysteria)

description_en: Dried root tuber of a Himalayan peony, used traditionally for epilepsy and nerve disorders.
safety_note: No human safety data found; an extract showed no general toxicity in brine shrimp, which is only a preliminary lab signal.
evidence_note: Only lab findings (antioxidant, lipoxygenase inhibition) are reported; no human clinical trials were found.

category_unani: Musammin-e-Badan (body fattening); Muqawwi-e-Bah (aphrodisiac); Muallid-e-Mani (semen producing); Munaffis-e-Balgam (expectorant)
description_en: Lint-free cotton seeds, used in Unani medicine as a nourishing tonic for weakness and low semen.
safety_note: Cottonseed contains gossypol, which is toxic and was studied as a male contraceptive because it can suppress sperm production, sometimes irreversibly; the monograph itself lists miscarriage and infertility. This conflicts with its traditional use for low semen.
evidence_note: Gossypol research was abandoned as a contraceptive due to toxicity and irreversibility; no evidence supports the fertility-promoting traditional use.

description_en: Seeds of a widely eaten gourd, used traditionally as a cooling remedy.
evidence_note: Wikipedia notes mainly traditional Ayurvedic use and nutrition data; no clinical evidence for the seeds was found.

description_en: The edible pistachio nut, used in Unani medicine as a nourishing tonic.
safety_note: Pistachios are a tree-nut allergen that can cause severe reactions including anaphylaxis; they contain urushiol-type irritants common to the cashew family and can be contaminated with aflatoxin.
evidence_note: An FDA qualified health claim says evidence suggests but does not prove nuts may reduce heart disease risk; reviews report modest blood pressure and triglyceride benefits.

category_unani: Musakkin-e-Alam (analgesic); Muhallil-e-Waram (anti-inflammatory); Mufarreh (exhilarant); Munaffis-e-Balgham (expectorant); Muallid-e-Mani (semen producing); Musammin-e-Badan (body fattening); Molayen (laxative)
description_en: Bark of the cluster fig tree, used in South Asian traditional medicine for diarrhoea, inflammation and tonics.
safety_note: The tree's milky latex can irritate skin. The monograph lists possible digestive-tract bleeding, sun sensitivity and rash, but I did not find independent confirmation.
evidence_note: Wikipedia cites no clinical or pharmacological evidence for bark use.

category_unani: Qabiz (astringent); Muqawwi-e-Meda (stomach tonic); Musakkin-e-Alam (analgesic); Munawwim (hypnotic); Mumsik (retentive)
description_en: Dried leaves of the cannabis plant, a psychoactive herb used in classical Unani and Ayurvedic medicine.
safety_note: NCCIH lists impaired driving, dizziness and falls, risk of psychosis in predisposed people, cannabis use disorder, cannabinoid hyperemesis, lower birth weight with use in pregnancy, and risk to children from accidental ingestion. In many countries the plant is a controlled substance.
evidence_note: FDA has approved specific cannabinoid drugs for some rare epilepsies, chemotherapy nausea and HIV-related appetite loss; evidence for diarrhoea, haemorrhoids or cough is not established.

description_en: Aromatic cassia cinnamon, a spice plant; the monograph lists the leaf, though the bark is the usual spice.
safety_note: Cassia contains coumarin, which can harm the liver at high or long-term intake and has a blood-thinning effect; European agencies advise limiting it. NCCIH notes possible interactions, skin irritation from oils, and caution with large amounts in pregnancy.
evidence_note: NCCIH says research does not clearly show cinnamon helps diabetes or weight loss; studies often fail to specify species or part.

category_unani: Muhallil-e-Waram (anti-inflammatory); Musakkin-e-Alam (analgesic); Muqawwi-e-Meda (stomach tonic); Muqawwi-e-Kabid (liver tonic); Munaffis-e-Balgham (expectorant)
description_en: Dried aromatic flower buds of a tropical tree, used as a spice and for toothache.
safety_note: Eugenol is toxic at high doses in test organisms; oral use may cause problems in people with liver disease, clotting disorders, immune disorders or food allergies. Clove can irritate gums and skin.
evidence_note: Evidence supports clove oil containing eugenol for toothache and some dry-socket pain; evidence for blood sugar, fever and other uses is inconclusive.

description_en: Safflower, a thistle-like plant grown for dye, oil and flowers; Unani texts use the flowers or seeds as medicine.
safety_note: No specific safety findings found in fetched sources; the usual caution to check with a clinician before use in pregnancy or with bleeding problems is general advice, not sourced.
evidence_note: Small trials show safflower oil lowers LDL cholesterol more than butter or lard; no clinical evidence was found for the flowers or the Unani uses.

botanical_name: Dolomiaea costus (syn. Saussurea costus, S. lappa)
category_unani: Jali (cleanser); Muhallil-e-Waram (anti-inflammatory); Muqawwi-e-Asab (nerve tonic); Munaffis-e-Balgam (expectorant); Mudirr-e-Boul (diuretic); Mudirr-e-Haiz (emmenagogue); Qatil-e-Deedan-e-A'ama (anthelmintic)
description_en: Aromatic root of a Himalayan herb, long used in Unani and Ayurvedic medicine and in incense.
safety_note: A 2019 case report links the root to a severe pustular skin reaction (AGEP) confirmed by patch testing. The monograph lists dizziness and nausea. The species is CITES Appendix I.
evidence_note: Claims rest mostly on traditional use and preclinical work; the monograph file lists Orchis mascula (salep) but its elevation and root description fit costus, so identity was inferred from the name Qust, not confirmed against the book.

description_en: The familiar edible turnip root, used traditionally as a food-medicine for cough and urinary complaints.
evidence_note: Wikipedia documents only culinary and agricultural use; no clinical evidence for the Unani uses was found.

category_unani: Muhallil-e-Waram (anti-inflammatory); Musakkin (sedative); Jali (cleanser); Mutayyib-e-Dahan (breath freshener); Muqawwi-e-Qalb (heart tonic); Muqawwi-e-Dimag (brain tonic); Mudirr-e-Boul (diuretic)
description_en: Aromatic rhizome of a Himalayan plant, used for centuries as a sedative, perfume and incense.
safety_note: The monograph advises avoiding it in pregnancy, lactation and known hypersensitivity; I found no independent safety data. The species is critically endangered and CITES-listed.
evidence_note: Chemistry research is described as preliminary and medicinal claims are traditional; no clinical studies were found.

category_unani: Mufatteh Sudad (deobstruent); Muhallil-e-Waram (anti-inflammatory); Muqawwi-e-Dimagh (brain tonic); Muqawwi-e-Asab (nerve tonic); Mudirr-e-Boul (diuretic); Mudirr-e-Haiz (emmenagogue)
description_en: Rhizome of a Himalayan valerian relative, used as a mild sedative and nerve tonic.
safety_note: Data are for European valerian generally: may cause drowsiness, headache, dizziness and rarely liver toxicity; can add to sedatives; avoid in pregnancy and stop a week before surgery (MSK). Not specific to this species.
evidence_note: Support is largely traditional; clinical trials of valerian for sleep are mixed and modest, and none specific to V. jatamansi were found.

description_en: Dried peel of the citron, a fragrant citrus fruit used traditionally against nausea.
evidence_note: Historical uses such as seasickness and scurvy are described as supposed; a 2025 review notes antimicrobial activity of its compounds, with no clinical evidence found.

description_en: Milky latex of a cactus-like spurge shrub, used in tiny drop doses in traditional medicine.
safety_note: Euphorbia latex in general is a caustic skin irritant and poisonous; no species-specific toxicity data were found, so treat the latex as hazardous.
evidence_note: Wikipedia gives no clinical evidence; only a purported snail-killing property and a link to the resin shilajit are noted.
